project1.title: Deadly Nightshade
project1.shortDescription: Technical Designer • Playable thesis game with 30+ minutes of content — narrative stealth-action, cinematic storytelling and custom AI systems
project1.outcome: Playable thesis game with 30+ minutes of content

content.title: Overview
content.text: Deadly Nightshade was my thesis project at IED Milano: a story about a future where nature and technology blend in really unsettling ways. You follow Alice, a young scientist, and Rusty, this little robot she secretly builds. When they escape from the lab together, they start uncovering some pretty dark truths about the company they used to trust, and along the way they form this beautiful bond that drives the whole story.

content.description: Main cover art for Deadly Nightshade.

content.title: My Role
content.text: I wore a lot of hats as the **Technical Designer** on this one. I jumped between **gameplay programming, AI systems, dialogue mechanics, audio integration, UI design, technical animation, and building custom tools**, basically making sure the technical side and the story worked together seamlessly.

content.description: Gameplay interaction demo video.

content.title: Artificial Intelligence & Enemies
content.text: Creating the **enemy AI** was really fun, I gave them different senses like sight and hearing, plus they react when they take damage. I also built this **custom spawn system** that changes based on what's happening in the environment. The bosses were especially interesting to work on: the **final boss** can actually target specific spots for jump attacks, while the **slimy boss** crawls up  and can make the floor collapse during fights. I also put together this **Waves Arena Game Mode** that throws progressively harder enemies at you.

content.description: Behavior tree example for enemy AI.

content.title: Dialogue & Narrative Tools
content.text: I built a **custom dialogue system** that lets Alice and Rusty talk to each other naturally throughout the game. The conversations trigger from all sorts of things,  walking into areas, taking damage, interacting with objects  and they flow right into cutscenes with subtitles. Everything connects to **FMOD** for the audio side. I also helped Giulia write the script and spent time in the **voice acting sessions** to make sure everything sounded just right.

content.description: Boss fight composition and effects.

content.title: Audio Integration
content.text: Getting **FMOD** working in the project was a big challenge: I set up dynamic systems for music, ambient sounds, interactive objects, and both 2D and 3D audio effects. I created specific nodes to control exactly how sounds behave. I also made this **Physics Material system** so you get different footstep sounds and impact effects depending on what surface you're walking on.

content.description: Audio trigger in editor for FMOD integration.

content.title: UI & Visual Design
content.text: I worked with [Christian](https://www.christiancatenacci.com/) to design UI pages in **Figma**, and I created the **game's logo** plus a bunch of graphics for both in-game and promotional stuff. One thing I'm particularly proud of is the **custom media system for Rusty's screen**, it plays video textures through the **BINK plugin** to show his emotions during gameplay and cutscenes.

content.description: In game UI design.

content.title: Technical Animation & Physics
content.text: I handled **Rusty's procedural physics** for his arms and legs, making them more or less stiff depending on whether you're playing or watching a cutscene. I worked on the **technical animation pipeline** too, setting up state machines and custom logic for enemies, bosses, and Alice (who uses the **Advanced Locomotion System** in C++). I also created **interactive props** like rotating valves, breakable crates, security cameras, metal detectors, and hidden compartments.

content.description: Showcase of enemy AI and behaviors.

content.title: Level Streaming & World Building
content.text: I set up **Level Streaming** for elevators, doors, and loading different areas dynamically - this keeps performance smooth by only loading what you need. It also meant everyone on the team could work on different areas without stepping on each other's toes through **Git**. I collaborated with [Christian](https://www.christiancatenacci.com/) on **Level Design**, working on rough layouts for places like the 'General Lab' and 'Green Dome', then refining them through lots of playtesting.

content.description: Map zones and level design overview.

content.title: Tools & Optimization
content.text: I wrote several **Python tools** to automate boring tasks: turning off sRGB on ARM textures in batches, finding unused meshes, spotting performance-heavy components, and automatically enabling 'Activate Only When Rendered'. These tools made a huge difference in both project performance and our workflow. I also helped get everything working properly on **Steam Deck**.

content.title: Visual Effects
content.text: I created some **VFX** myself, like the final boss stomp effect and enemy explosion effects. [Christian](https://www.christiancatenacci.com/) and I also picked and integrated other VFX throughout the project to make both the atmosphere and gameplay moments really pop.

content.description: Showcase of final boss VFX and effects.

content.title: Collaboration & Outcome
content.text: We built Deadly Nightshade in **Unreal Engine 5.4** for our thesis, and ended up with a fully playable game with over 30 minutes of content. Beyond all the technical stuff, I also worked as **co-director and co-writer**, making sure the story, design, and systems all worked together. Finishing this in July 2025 was honestly one of the most challenging and rewarding things I've done in game development so far.

project2.title: Juan The Game
project2.shortDescription: Solo Developer • 60+ handcrafted levels shipped — physics-based mobile puzzle with custom horse character designs

content.title: Overview
content.text: **Juan The Game** is this quirky physics-based mobile puzzle game where you guide a horse through levels by making him fall perfectly into balconies. What started as just a fun side project with a friend turned into this full mobile experience with over **60 unique levels**  and I'm still adding new ones because it's just too much fun to stop.

content.description: Juan The Game Trailer showcasing gameplay and mechanics.

content.title: Technical Implementation
content.text: I built it in **Unity** with **C#**, using Unity's physics system with custom **Rigidbody** components on different parts of the horse  his legs, tail, body segments, everything. This creates these hilarious and realistic physics interactions that make the core gameplay work. Getting the physics to feel just right was tricky  you want it realistic enough to be believable but fun enough that it doesn't frustrate players.

content.description: Physics-based gameplay demonstration across multiple levels.

content.title: Solo Development
content.text: I pretty much handled everything: **Programming** the gameplay mechanics and physics, **designing all 60+ levels** with careful attention to how difficulty ramps up, creating **custom horse skins** and character art, and designing the **UI/UX** to make sure mobile controls felt intuitive and players always knew what was happening.

content.description: Unity editor showing level design and horse rig.

content.title: Level Design & Player Experience
content.text: Every single level was hand-crafted to give players a unique challenge while keeping that learning curve smooth. I spent a lot of time collecting **player feedback** and learned some hard lessons about what makes challenges fun versus what just makes people want to throw their phone. That feedback loop made me redesign tons of levels, which taught me how important **iterative design** and actually listening to users really is.

content.description: Juan The Game main menu showcasing custom horse character.

content.title: Art & Visual Identity
content.text: Beyond all the programming, I drew all the **custom horse skins** and character designs, giving players different ways to personalize their experience. This was my chance to dive into **digital illustration** and **character design**, plus I learned how to get artwork to look good in Unity's rendering system.

content.description: Shop showing different horse skins available.

content.title: Learning Outcomes
content.text: This year-long project taught me so much about **mobile game development**, **physics programming**, and especially **how to actually use player feedback** instead of just collecting it. I learned when to hold players' hands and guide them versus when to let them figure things out, and how to tell the difference between a good challenge and something that just makes people quit.

content.title: Code Example

project5.title: Echoes Card Game
project5.shortDescription: Game Designer • 2-4 player tabletop prototype validated via playtests — strategic disruption mechanics on classic Memory
project5.outcome: 2-4 player tabletop prototype validated via playtests

content.title: Game Design Innovation
content.text: **Echoes** takes the classic Memory card game and adds this twist where you can actually mess with your opponents' progress. Instead of just quietly matching pairs, you can play special effect cards to shuffle things around and make it way harder for other players to complete their matches. It supports 2-4 players and creates these really tense, competitive moments.

content.description: Echoes card game box and complete component set.

content.title: Core Mechanics
content.text: We kept the basic matching foundation that everyone knows, but added **special effect cards** that let you shuffle the field and disrupt other players. This creates this interesting balance where pure memory skills aren't enough you also need to think about timing, when to play your disruption cards, and how to read what your opponents are up to.

content.description: Drawings and sketches from the design process.

content.title: Victory Conditions & Strategy
content.text: You win by being the **first to get rid of all your cards** through successful matching. But with the interference mechanics, it's not just about remembering where cards are  you need to develop **timing strategies**, learn to **assess risks**, and figure out when your opponents are close to winning so you can deploy disruption cards at the right moment.

content.description: Game in progress showing card layout and player interaction.

content.title: Design Process & Iteration
content.text: This was a university project I worked on with a partner, and we went through tons of design iterations. We spent a lot of time **playtesting and balancing** to make sure the disruption mechanics made the game more fun rather than just frustrating. The whole process taught me a lot about **how to playtest properly** and **iterative game design**.

content.description: Echoes card game box and complete component set.

content.title: Production & Manufacturing
content.text: We actually made this into a **real physical product**, which meant figuring out **print design**, **component quality**, and **packaging**. I used **Adobe Creative Suite** for the visual design, and learned a lot about **print production workflows** and how digital designs translate when you actually print them on physical game components.

content.description: Box front design showcasing logo and artwork.

content.title: User Reception & Validation
content.text: After we finished production, we playtested Echoes extensively and got **really positive feedback** from our peer group. The success validated our design decisions and proved that our approach to reimagining a classic game actually worked. This experience taught me how important **user feedback** is for validating game design decisions.

content.description: Developing the game in team

project6.title: Too Poop To Go
project6.shortDescription: Web Developer • Cross-platform restroom finder — mobile apps, admin dashboard and OTP-secured moderation workflows

content.title: Project Overview
content.text: **Too Poop To Go** is a platform to help people find the best public restrooms when they really need them. This was a team project with **Android and iOS mobile apps** built by my teammates, and I developed the entire **web management system** from scratch. Together it creates this complete ecosystem for crowdsourced restroom information.

content.description: Too Poop To Go web management dashboard overview.

content.title: My Technical Role
content.text: I handled the entire **front-end web management system** using **React** and **Tailwind CSS**, creating a responsive interface that actually feels good to use. I also **worked on the backend** with **Django**, helping with API design, database planning, and server-side logic.

content.description: Poop streak feature.

content.title: Web Management Features
content.text: The web system gives administrators complete control: **User management** where you can view, ban, or remove users; **Review moderation** to view and delete inappropriate reviews across all restrooms; **Restroom approval system** for processing user submissions; **Interactive map interface** showing all existing restrooms; and **Tag management** for organizing and categorizing restroom features.

content.title: Authentication & Security
content.text: We built a solid **user authentication system** with **OTP (One-Time Password) verification** for extra security. The system includes **secure login flows**, **session management**, and **role-based access control** so only authorized administrators can access sensitive platform data and controls.

content.description: Too Poop To Go web management dashboard overview.

content.title: Map Integration
content.text: The whole platform uses **MapBox APIs**, both the mobile apps and web management system, so everything works consistently and reliably. I designed the web interface to integrate map interactions smoothly, letting administrators visualize restroom locations, see geographical distribution, and manage location-based data efficiently.

content.description: Otp Mail verification system.

content.title: Approval Workflow System
content.text: One of the key features I built is the **restroom approval workflow**,  when users submit new locations through the mobile apps, they show up in the admin dashboard for review. This includes **detailed submission information**, **image verification**, **location accuracy checking**, and **streamlined approval/rejection processes** with notifications back to the mobile apps.

content.title: Team Collaboration
content.text: Working with a team of three, I made sure the mobile apps and web management system integrated seamlessly through **RESTful API design** and **consistent data structures**. This meant constantly communicating with the mobile developers to coordinate **data formatting**, **error handling**, and **real-time synchronization** between platforms.

content.title: Technical Skills Developed
content.text: This project really advanced my skills in **React development**, **responsive web design**, **API integration**, **state management**, **Django backend development**, and **collaborative software development**. I gained valuable experience in **project coordination**, **version control with Git**, and **agile development** while working in a multi-developer environment.

content.description: Cross platform simple diagram.

project3.title: The Friend Archive
project3.shortDescription: Solo Developer • Live shared catalogue for movies, series, books and games — Next.js App Router, Supabase auth and per-member progress
project3.outcome: Live shared catalogue for movies, series, books and games

content.title: Overview
content.text: **The Friend Archive** is a shared catalogue for everything worth experiencing together: **movies, TV series, books, and video games**. You create a group with your friends, you fill it with the things you want to watch, read, or play, and everyone tracks their own progress through the same list. It solves a problem I actually had  nobody ever remembers what the group already watched, or what someone recommended three months ago. The tagline sums it up: **Track together. Remember always.**

content.title: Architecture
content.text: It's a **Next.js 15** app on the **App Router**, written in **TypeScript** and deployed on **Vercel**, with **Supabase** (PostgreSQL) behind it. Server Components are the default and I only opt into Client Components where interactivity actually needs it. The rule I held myself to: database queries live in Server Components, Server Actions, or route handlers  never in a Client Component  and the Supabase client is only ever created in two files, one for the browser and one for the server. It sounds pedantic, but it's what keeps the data layer from leaking everywhere as the app grows.

content.title: Data Model
content.text: The schema is **nine tables** in three layers: identity (`profiles`, `subscriptions`), organisation (`groups`, `group_members`, `group_join_requests`), and content (`media_items`, `item_statuses`, `consumption_records`, `comments`). The decision I'm happiest with is that **status is per-member**: `media_items` has no status column at all, because a group's copy of **Dune** isn't watched  **you** watched it. Each member gets their own row in `item_statuses`, and a missing row just means Planned. Type-specific fields (director, author, developer, seasons) live in a **JSONB metadata** column, so adding a fifth media type doesn't mean a migration full of mostly-null columns.

content.title: Authentication & Row Level Security
content.text: Auth is **Supabase Auth** with email and password, and `middleware.ts` refreshes the session on every request through `@supabase/ssr`. The part that took the most thought was **Row Level Security**: the business rules aren't just checked in the UI, they're enforced by **RLS policies in the database**, so they hold even if someone talks to the API directly. Every write to a status row is restricted to `user_id = auth.uid()`, and an RLS policy makes `added_by` immutable after creation  you can't rewrite who added something.

content.description: Sign-in screen — Supabase email and password auth.

content.title: External Metadata Providers
content.text: Nobody wants to type in a film's director by hand, so adding an item searches an external provider and fills the metadata for you. Each media type routes to a different one: **TMDB** for movies and TV series, **Open Library** for books, and **RAWG** for video games. They all normalise into a single internal shape, so the rest of the app only ever speaks one language regardless of who answered. The searches go through a **server-side route handler** that requires a session, which keeps the API keys off the client and stops the proxy being open to the world. Every provider call resolves rather than throws: if one is down, you get an empty list and fall back to typing it in yourself.

content.title: Groups & Collaboration
content.text: A group has an **owner** and **members**  no other roles, deliberately. Owners manage the group and its membership; members add items, edit them, and write their own notes and comments. Groups are **public or private**: public ones are discoverable and readable by anyone signed in, but non-members see them **read-only**, and joining goes through a **request and approval flow** rather than just walking in. Each item carries shared **comments** and **tags**, plus per-member notes on the consumption record  the same film gets one note from you and a different one from your friend. When every current member has completed an item, it gets a star.

content.title: Working Inside the Free Tier
content.text: The whole thing runs on free tiers, which turned out to be a useful design constraint rather than an annoyance. No `select('*')`  every query names its columns. Related data comes back through **nested selects** in one round-trip instead of an N+1 fan-out. No polling, and no Realtime subscriptions unless a feature genuinely needs live updates (so far, none do). Stable reference data gets cached client-side rather than refetched on every render. Being forced to justify each query made the app faster than it would have been with an unlimited budget.

content.title: Design System
content.text: The frontend runs on a token system in `globals.css`  semantic names for colour, radius, shadow, spacing, duration, easing  and no ad-hoc hex values in component files. Components are built on **Radix UI** primitives following the shadcn pattern, styled with **Tailwind CSS 4**, with **Framer Motion** for transitions that stay under ~350ms so they add spatial clarity without making you wait. Loading states use **skeletons shaped like the real layout** instead of blank flashes, and async buttons show an inline spinner and disable themselves.

content.title: Learning Outcomes
content.text: This is the project where **Postgres stopped being 'the database' and became part of the design**. Pushing rules into RLS instead of trusting the UI, modelling status per-member instead of per-item, choosing JSONB where the shape genuinely varies  those decisions shaped the app more than any component did. It's still in active development, and the schema has held up to every feature I've added since, which is the best signal I could ask for.

project4.title: Sudoku NFC
project4.shortDescription: Solo Developer • Published on Google Play — write Sudoku puzzles to physical NFC tags and scan them to play

content.title: Overview
content.text: **Sudoku NFC** turns cheap **NFC tags into playable Sudoku cards**. You create a puzzle in the app, write it to a tag, and from then on tapping your phone against that tag loads the puzzle and drops you straight into playing it. The idea was to give a digital puzzle a physical object to live on  a stack of tags on your desk becomes a stack of Sudokus you can hand to someone. It's built with **Expo** and **React Native**, and it's on **Google Play**.

content.description: Home screen and the scan-to-play flow waiting for a tag.

content.title: Getting a Sudoku Onto a Tag
content.text: This was the fun constraint. A cheap **NTAG213** tag holds about **144 bytes**, so there was no room for JSON, metadata, or anything clever. A puzzle is stored as a raw **81-character string** (digits, `0` for empty), and multiple puzzles are packed with a single comma between them  no prefixes, no wrappers. That's **81 bytes per puzzle**, 82 for each one after the first. The app does the arithmetic both ways: it can tell you how many bytes a set of puzzles needs, and how many puzzles will actually fit in a given tag's capacity, so a write fails before it starts rather than halfway through.

content.title: Writing & Reading Tags
content.text: Everything goes through **NDEF** text records with `react-native-nfc-manager`. Before any of that, the app checks whether the device even supports NFC and whether it's switched on, and offers to open the system settings if it isn't. On **Android** an intent filter for `NDEF_DISCOVERED` means the OS can hand the app a tag directly, and scans can be cancelled mid-flight instead of hanging. Reading is deliberately forgiving: every puzzle on the tag is validated on the way in, malformed ones are collected as errors instead of crashing the scan, and anything that isn't a well-formed puzzle simply doesn't load.

content.description: Three ways to create a puzzle, and the manual 9x9 grid editor.

content.title: Three Ways to Make a Puzzle
content.text: You can **paste an 81-character string**, **fill a 9x9 grid by hand**, or **generate one automatically**. The manual editor validates as you go and shows conflicts live, because finding out your hand-built puzzle was broken only after writing it to a tag would be miserable. Puzzles queue up in a **write buffer** so you can build several and commit them to a tag in one tap, with the capacity check deciding how many actually fit.

content.title: The Sudoku Engine
content.text: The engine is the biggest module in the project and it's plain JavaScript with no dependencies. Generation starts from a **complete solution built by backtracking**, then removes clues while checking the puzzle stays solvable. The part I'm proudest of is **difficulty**: instead of counting clues  which barely correlates with how hard a puzzle feels  it scores a puzzle by **solving it the way a person would**, using singles techniques, and grades it from the effort that takes. The score maps to **Easy, Medium, Hard, or Expert**, and a puzzle that can't be cracked that way is Expert by definition. Generation then retries until it lands in the difficulty band you asked for.

content.title: Playing
content.text: The board itself is a normal, comfortable Sudoku: a number pad, **pencil marks** for candidates, conflict highlighting, and locked cells you can't overwrite. You can **verify your solution** at any point, or reset and start the puzzle over. The helpers are optional and live in settings  **timer**, **region highlighting**, and **error checking**  so you can play with training wheels or without. There's haptic feedback on input, and puzzles you've scanned are kept locally so a tag you've already read stays playable.

content.title: Learning Outcomes
content.text: Two things stuck. First, **hardware constraints make better design**: 144 bytes killed every over-engineered format I considered and left something that's trivial to read, write, and debug. Second, **shipping is its own skill**  icons, adaptive icons, permission strings, store listing, versioning, an actual release build. Getting it onto **Google Play** taught me more about the last mile of mobile development than the code did.

project7.title: AR iPad Experience
project7.shortDescription: AR Developer • Confidential iPad AR app delivered under NDA — marker tracking, 3D asset integration and real-time mobile rendering
project7.outcome: Confidential iPad AR app delivered under NDA

content.title: Overview
content.text: This one is covered by an **NDA**, so I can't show the client, the artwork, or what the app is actually for. What I can talk about is the engineering: it's an **augmented reality iPad application** built in **Unity** with the **Vuforia Engine**, where you point the tablet at a real-world target and the digital content anchors onto it and stays there while you move around. Everything below is about how that was built, not about what it shows.

content.title: My Role
content.text: I implemented the **AR experience end to end**: target tracking, object placement, the **UI**, the animations, and the overall **project architecture**. Working under NDA meant being careful about what left the repo, but internally it was a normal Unity project with all the usual constraints  and a few extra ones that come with running AR on a tablet.

content.title: Tracking & Spatial Positioning
content.text: The core challenge was making virtual objects feel like they actually belong in the room. I worked with **Vuforia's** tracking to anchor content to real-world targets, then spent a lot of time on **object positioning in AR space**  getting scale, orientation, and offsets right so things sit where you expect them to. Tracking never behaves perfectly in the real world: lighting changes, people move the tablet too fast, targets get partially covered. I handled the **recovery and re-anchoring** cases so the experience degrades gracefully instead of having objects pop or drift away.

content.title: 3D Assets & Render Performance
content.text: I integrated the **3D assets** into the scene and got them running smoothly on **iOS** hardware, which is where most of the work went. AR is expensive: the camera feed, the tracking, and the rendering are all fighting for the same frame budget, and dropping frames in AR doesn't just look bad, it breaks the illusion that the object is really there. I worked through **draw calls, material and texture setup, mesh complexity, and lighting** to keep **real-time rendering** stable on the device rather than just in the editor.

content.title: UI, Buttons & Animation
content.text: I designed and implemented the **interface** on top of the AR view: the **buttons**, the states, and the **animations** that tie them together. AR UI is its own problem  the camera feed behind it is unpredictable, so contrast and placement have to hold up against whatever the user happens to be pointing at. I kept the transitions short and readable so the interface guides you without ever competing with the AR content itself.

content.title: Architecture & Asset Organization
content.text: I set up the **project architecture** from the start: **folder structure**, naming, prefab organization, and how **assets and resources** were managed across the project. This is the boring part that nobody sees, but on a project with a lot of incoming 3D content it's what keeps things from turning into a mess. Clean organization plus **Git** meant changes stayed reviewable and the build stayed predictable as the asset count grew.

content.title: Learning Outcomes
content.text: This project taught me a lot about **AR development** specifically: how different it is to debug something that only misbehaves in physical space, and how much **mobile performance** work AR really demands. It also pushed me on **architecture discipline**  when you can't share screenshots or ask the internet about your exact problem, the structure of your own project is what saves you.

project8.title: Cross-Platform Content App
project8.shortDescription: Full-Stack Developer • Confidential iOS and Android app delivered under NDA — publishing, rating and commenting on user-generated content
project8.outcome: Confidential iOS and Android app delivered under NDA

content.title: Overview
content.text: Another **NDA** project, so no client, no screenshots, and nothing about what people actually post on it. In technical terms it's a **cross-platform mobile app** built with **Flutter** and backed by **Firebase**: users publish their own content, and other users can **rate and comment** on it. One codebase, shipping to both **iOS** and **Android**.

content.title: My Role
content.text: I worked **full-stack** on this: the **Flutter** client, the **Firebase** backend, the **authentication**, and the **application architecture** that holds it together. Being responsible for both sides meant I could design the data model and the UI against each other instead of negotiating an API in the middle, which made a lot of decisions faster.

content.title: Application Architecture
content.text: I set up the **architecture** early: how state flows through the app, where the Firebase calls live, and how the UI stays decoupled from the data layer so screens stay testable and easy to change. User-generated content means the app is basically never in a static state  things get posted, rated, and commented on while you're looking at them  so the structure had to make **reactive updates** the normal case rather than a special one.

content.title: Firebase Backend
content.text: The whole backend runs on **Firebase**. I designed the **data model** around the read patterns rather than the write ones, because a content feed reads constantly and writes rarely, and modelling it the wrong way around gets expensive fast. That covered how content, ratings, and comments relate to each other, how aggregate scores stay consistent, and **security rules** so users can only touch what's actually theirs.

content.title: Authentication & Login
content.text: I implemented **authentication and login**, including the account flows, session persistence across app launches, and the states around them  signed out, signing in, signed in, and all the failure cases in between. On a platform where everything is tied to a user identity, auth isn't a screen you build once and forget: it's the thing every other feature quietly depends on.

content.title: Ratings & Comments
content.text: The social layer is what makes the app work: users **rate** and **comment** on what other people publish, and that feedback has to show up quickly and consistently. I built these so the interface responds immediately while the backend catches up, and so the same content looks the same whichever device you open it on.

content.title: Cross-Platform Development
content.text: Shipping one **Flutter** codebase to **iOS** and **Android** is a huge time saver, but it isn't free  the two platforms disagree about permissions, keyboards, navigation gestures, and plenty of small behaviours that only show up on real devices. I tested against both throughout instead of treating one as the main platform and the other as a port.

content.title: Learning Outcomes
content.text: This project pushed my **Flutter** and **Firebase** skills a long way, especially around **data modelling** and **authentication**. The bigger lesson was about user-generated content: the moment real people can publish, rate, and comment, the edge cases stop being hypothetical, and you learn to design for them up front instead of patching them later.
